# @concept: least-privilege
# 1. Least privilege: the token these jobs get can only READ the repo. No job here needs more.
permissions:
  contents: read

# 2. One run per branch at a time: a new push cancels the older, now useless, run.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: http://localhost:4000

# @concept: docker-layer-caching
      # 3. Build the API image. `push: false` = build only, so a broken Dockerfile fails CI
      #    but nothing is published. `context: .` is the repo root (the Dockerfile needs several folders).
      #    cache-from / cache-to: store the layers in the GitHub Actions cache, so the next run reuses
      #    unchanged layers (like the pnpm install) instead of rebuilding them. mode=max also stores
      #    the layers of the build stages that are not part of the final image. `scope` keeps the
      #    API and web caches apart so they do not overwrite each other.
      - name: Build API image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          file: apps/api/Dockerfile
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: minitickets-ci-api:scan
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=api

#
# @concept: docker-multi-stage
# Stages (each starts with FROM; later stages copy only what they need from earlier ones):
#   base    -> Node + pnpm. A shared starting point, produces no files of its own.
#   deps    -> ALL dependencies installed (dev tools too). Produces node_modules for the build.
#   build   -> runs esbuild. Produces dist/server.js and dist/migrate.js (plain JavaScript).
#   prod    -> ONLY production dependencies. Produces a small node_modules for runtime.
#   runtime -> the final image. dist/ + prod node_modules + SQL migrations. Nothing else.
# Only the last stage becomes the image we run. The others are thrown away, which is why it is small.

# 1. WHAT: start from the official Node image, the "slim" (Debian) variant, pinned to an exact version.
#    WHY: the build toolchain matches .nvmrc (24.13.0); runtime gets newer patches within Node 24.
#    "slim" has Node and little else (small), and it is glibc-based, which the prebuilt
#    @node-rs/argon2 binary needs (Alpine uses musl and is a common source of native-package trouble).
FROM node:24.13.0-slim AS base

# 2. WHAT: turn on corepack and activate the pnpm version written in the root package.json.

# @concept: docker-layer-caching
# 4. WHAT: copy ONLY the files that decide which packages to install: the lockfile,
#    the workspace file and the package.json of every workspace package.
#    WHY (layer caching): Docker caches each instruction as a layer and reuses it if its input
#    did not change. If we copied all the source code first, every code edit would change the
#    input and force a full re-install. The package files change rarely, so the slow install
#    layer below is reused on almost every build.
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml ./
COPY apps/api/package.json apps/api/package.json
COPY packages/shared/package.json packages/shared/package.json

# 5. WHAT: install the API's dependencies (dev ones included, we need esbuild) exactly as the lockfile says.
#    `--filter @minitickets/api...` means "the api and the packages it depends on", so the web
#    app's packages are skipped. --frozen-lockfile fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree.
#    WHY: the cache mount keeps pnpm's download store between builds, so even when the package
#    files change, packages already downloaded are not downloaded again. The mount is not part

# @concept: tls-in-transit
# 11b. WHAT: download AWS's RDS certificate bundle (the certificate authorities, CAs, that sign
#      every RDS database certificate, in all regions) and tell Node to trust it as well.
#      WHY: on AWS the API connects to RDS with SSL and VERIFIES the certificate (see
#      src/config/database.ts). Node only trusts the well-known public CAs, and the RDS CA is
#      not one of them, so without this file the check fails with "self-signed certificate in
#      certificate chain". The fix is to trust AWS's CA, NEVER to turn the check off.
#      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS ADDS these CAs to Node's normal list (public sites still work).
#      --chmod=644: files downloaded by ADD are readable only by root by default, and the app
#      runs as the "node" user (step 15). The target folder /usr/local/share already exists:
#      ADD would create a missing folder with the same 644 mode, and nobody could open it.
#      It is harmless locally: the local Postgres uses no SSL, so these CAs are never used there.
#      Docker checks the URL on every build, so a new bundle from AWS lands in the next image.
ADD --chmod=644 https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem /usr/local/share/rds-global-bundle.pem
ENV NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/usr/local/share/rds-global-bundle.pem

# @concept: container-hardening
# 15. WHAT: switch from root to the "node" user (already in the official image, uid 1000).
#     WHY: if someone breaks into the app, they get a user that cannot change the system or
#     install tools, instead of root inside the container.
USER node

# 16. WHAT: document that the API listens on port 4000.
#     WHY: it does not open the port by itself; it tells people and tools which port to publish
#     (docker-compose.yml does that with `ports`).
EXPOSE 4000

# @concept: graceful-shutdown
# 17. WHAT: start the server by running node directly, in "exec form" (a JSON list).
#     WHY: with this form node is PID 1, the process Docker sends signals to. `docker stop`
#     sends SIGTERM straight to node, so our graceful shutdown in server.ts runs. With
#     `pnpm start` or the string form (CMD node ...), a shell or pnpm would be PID 1 and

# @concept: graceful-shutdown
# 17. WHAT: start the server by running node directly, in "exec form" (a JSON list).
#     WHY: with this form node is PID 1, the process Docker sends signals to. `docker stop`
#     sends SIGTERM straight to node, so our graceful shutdown in server.ts runs. With
#     `pnpm start` or the string form (CMD node ...), a shell or pnpm would be PID 1 and
#     would not pass SIGTERM on, so Docker would wait 10 seconds and then kill the app.
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

// 1. TIME gives every API task the same clock. Refill and consume happen in one atomic script.
// @concept: rate-limiting
export const TAKE_TOKEN = `
local time = redis.call('TIME')
local now = tonumber(time[1]) * 1000 + math.floor(tonumber(time[2]) / 1000)
local capacity, interval = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2])
local old = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'at')
local at = tonumber(old[2]) or now
now = math.max(now, at)
local tokens = math.min(capacity, (tonumber(old[1]) or capacity) + (now - at) / interval)
local allowed, retry = 0, 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1; allowed = 1
else retry = math.ceil((1 - tokens) * interval) end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'at', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity * interval))
return {allowed, retry}
`;

#
# @concept: docker-multi-stage
# Stages (only the last one becomes the image we run):
#   base    -> Node + pnpm. A shared starting point, produces no files of its own.
#   deps    -> ALL dependencies installed. Produces node_modules for the build.
#   build   -> runs `next build`. Produces .next/standalone (a tiny self-contained server).
#   runtime -> the final image. Only the standalone server, the static files and public/.

# 1. WHAT: official Node "slim" image, pinned to the exact version in .nvmrc.
#    WHY: keep the laptop/CI build toolchain; runtime gets newer patches within Node 24. Slim keeps it small.
FROM node:24.13.0-slim AS base

# 2. WHAT: enable corepack and activate the pnpm version from the root package.json.
#    WHY: the build stages need pnpm, and the same version as the repo gives the same install.
RUN corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@10.33.2 --activate

# 3. WHAT: set the folder where the next instructions run.

# @concept: docker-layer-caching
# 4. WHAT: copy only the files that decide which packages to install.
#    WHY (layer caching): the install below is slow. Docker reuses a layer when its input is
#    unchanged. Package files change rarely; source code changes all the time. Copying only
#    the package files first means a code edit does not repeat the install.
#    The web app imports TYPES from the API (type AppRouter), so the api package.json is needed too.
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml ./
COPY apps/web/package.json apps/web/package.json
COPY apps/api/package.json apps/api/package.json
COPY packages/shared/package.json packages/shared/package.json

# 5. WHAT: install the web app's dependencies and those of the packages it needs, exactly as in the lockfile.
#    WHY: --frozen-lockfile fails if the lockfile is out of date, so the image can never get
#    different versions than CI tested. The cache mount keeps pnpm's download store between
#    builds (it is not part of the image, so it adds no size).
RUN --mount=type=cache,id=pnpm-store,target=/root/.local/share/pnpm/store \

# @concept: twelve-factor-config
# 6. WHAT: declare a build argument and turn it into an environment variable.
#    WHY: Next.js copies NEXT_PUBLIC_* values INTO the JavaScript sent to browsers while it
#    builds. The value must therefore exist at BUILD time, and changing it later means a new
#    image. It is a public address, not a secret.
#    The default is EMPTY on purpose: empty means "call /trpc on the same origin as the page".
#    On AWS a load balancer routes /trpc/* to the api (Step 11f), so no address is baked in
#    and one image works everywhere. docker compose still passes the localhost URL.
ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=""
# 6b. WHAT: the ENV line below copies the ARG into an environment variable.
#     WHY: `next build` reads environment variables, not build arguments.
ENV NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=$NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL

# 7. WHAT: copy the sources, plus tsconfig.base.json (every package's tsconfig.json extends it).
#    Next needs the API source too, only for its TypeScript types.
#    WHY: after the install, so editing code does not invalidate the install layer above.

# @concept: container-hardening
# 15. WHAT: switch from root to the "node" user (already in the official image).
#     WHY: if someone breaks into the app, they cannot change the system. The files stay
#     owned by root and are only readable, so the app cannot rewrite its own code either.
USER node

# 16. WHAT: document that the web server listens on port 3000.
#     WHY: it only informs people and tools; docker-compose.yml's `ports` really publishes it.
EXPOSE 3000

# @concept: graceful-shutdown
# 17. WHAT: start the standalone server with node directly, in "exec form".
#     WHY: node becomes PID 1, so `docker stop` delivers SIGTERM straight to it and it exits
#     at once. Through pnpm or a shell, the signal would not arrive.
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# @concept: graceful-shutdown
# 17. WHAT: start the standalone server with node directly, in "exec form".
#     WHY: node becomes PID 1, so `docker stop` delivers SIGTERM straight to it and it exits
#     at once. Through pnpm or a shell, the signal would not arrive.
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

#
# @concept: docker-multi-stage
# Stages (same idea as apps/api/Dockerfile):
#   base    -> Node + pnpm, to BUILD. Never shipped.
#   deps    -> the worker's dependencies installed (dev tools too: esbuild).
#   build   -> esbuild bundles everything into ONE file: dist/lambda.mjs.
#   runtime -> AWS's Lambda base image + that one file. Nothing else.

# 1. WHAT: the build stages start from the same Node image as the api (pinned to .nvmrc's version).
#    WHY: same Node and pnpm as the laptop and CI, and Docker reuses the api build's cached layers.
FROM node:24.13.0-slim AS base
RUN corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@10.33.2 --activate
WORKDIR /app


# ---- Stage: deps ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
FROM base AS deps

# @concept: docker-layer-caching
# 2. WHAT: copy only the files that decide which packages to install, then install the worker and
#    the packages it depends on (`--filter @minitickets/worker...`), exactly as the lockfile says.
#    WHY: this slow layer is reused until a package.json or the lockfile changes.
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml ./
COPY apps/worker/package.json apps/worker/package.json
COPY packages/shared/package.json packages/shared/package.json
RUN --mount=type=cache,id=pnpm-store,target=/root/.local/share/pnpm/store \
    pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --filter @minitickets/worker...


# ---- Stage: build --------------------------------------------------------------------------
FROM deps AS build

# 3. WHAT: copy the worker's and the shared package's source, then bundle (apps/worker/build.mjs).
#    WHY: each dist/*.mjs bundle holds its handler AND every library it uses, so the final image

# ---- Stage: runtime (the final image) ------------------------------------------------------
# @concept: aws-lambda
# 4. WHAT: AWS's official base image for Lambda's Node.js 24 runtime ("nodejs24.x").
#    WHY this one: a CONTAINER-IMAGE Lambda must contain Lambda's "runtime interface client" (the
#      small program that fetches events from the Lambda service and calls our handler). AWS's base
#      images have it built in, plus a local emulator for testing (see PENDING.md, S1c).
#    WHY Node 24: .nvmrc says 24.13.0, and Lambda's newest Node runtime is 24 (Node 24.21.0 inside
#      the image when this was written). Same MAJOR version = same language features and APIs. Lambda
#      does not let us pick the minor/patch: AWS patches it, which is also the point (security fixes).
#    WHY the tag "24" (not a digest): AWS rebuilds this tag with security patches; every publish
#      (cd.yml) takes the current one. The pushed image itself never changes afterwards (immutable
#      tag), so a deploy still runs exactly the bytes CI built.
#    ARCHITECTURE: built with --platform linux/arm64 (cd.yml, scripts/push-images.sh) to match the
#      Lambda's "arm64" (Graviton) setting, infra/src/jobs/worker-lambda.ts. A mismatch fails at
#      start with "exec format error".
FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/nodejs:24 AS runtime

# @concept: migrations
  # One-off job: applies the SQL migrations, then exits. It is separate from the api on purpose:
  # if several api containers ran migrations at startup, they would race each other.
  migrate:
    # 1. build: make the image from our Dockerfile instead of downloading one.
    #    `context: .` is the repo root (the Dockerfile copies files from several folders);
    #    `dockerfile` says which Dockerfile inside that context.
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: apps/api/Dockerfile
    # image: the name given to the built image, so it is easy to find with `docker images`
    #        and so migrate and api share one name.
    image: minitickets-api
    # 2. profiles: a service with a profile starts only when that profile is asked for.
    #    So plain `pnpm db:up` still starts only postgres and redis.
    profiles: ["app"]

condition: service_healthy
    # @concept: health-checks
    # 5. healthcheck: the slim image has no curl, so use node to call /health. This lets
    #    `up --wait` and `depends_on` know when the API really answers.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:4000/health').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  web:
    # 1. build.args: values for the ARG lines in the Dockerfile. NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is copied into
    #    the browser JavaScript at build time, so it is the API address as the BROWSER sees it
    #    (the published port 4100), not the compose network name.
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: apps/web/Dockerfile

- "3100:3000"
    # @concept: server-to-server-calls
    # 3. environment: read by the web SERVER when a request comes in (not baked into the image).
    #    API_INTERNAL_URL is where the web server calls the API to render /events. Server to server,
    #    so it uses the compose service name "api" and the container port 4000, unlike the
    #    browser's NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL above (localhost:4100, the address the BROWSER sees).
    #    REVALIDATE_SECRET: what the api must send to POST /api/revalidate (the same root .env value).
    environment:
      API_INTERNAL_URL: http://api:4000
      REVALIDATE_SECRET: ${REVALIDATE_SECRET}
    # 4. depends_on: start after the API is healthy, so the first page load can already log in.
    #    The api calls the web too (the revalidate hook), but only when an event is created, never
    #    at startup, so it needs no depends_on on web (that would be a circle).
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy

# @concept: monorepo
# Tells pnpm which folders are packages in this monorepo.
packages:
  - "apps/*"
  - "packages/*"
  - "infra"

# 1. Drizzle Kit's legacy TS loader uses only esbuild's transform API. Keep that one
#    dependency on the patched version already used by Drizzle Kit itself.
overrides:
  "@esbuild-kit/core-utils@3.3.2>esbuild": "0.25.12"

# 1. Stop at the first error and on unset variables: a guard that fails must REFUSE, never pass.
# @concept: release-guard
set -euo pipefail

: "${CHECKED:?}" "${RECORDED:?}"
MAIN_TIP="${MAIN_TIP:-}"
ALLOW_OLDER="${ALLOW_OLDER:-false}"

# 2. refuse <message>: one ::error:: line, then exit 1 (the deploy stops before anything changes).
refuse() {
  echo "::error::$1"
  exit 1
}

# 3. Full 40-character ids, so "6ea9575" and its full id compare as the same commit.
CHECKED="$(git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$CHECKED^{commit}")" || refuse "Commit $CHECKED is not in the checked-out history."
SHORT="${CHECKED:0:7}"

# @concept: immutable-image-tags
# 4. WHAT: the tag is the short git SHA, e.g. 9fa3c21. Never "latest".
#    WHY: "latest" is a moving name: you cannot tell which code it holds, and it cannot be
#    used here at all because the repositories are IMMUTABLE (a tag can be pushed only once).
#    A SHA names exactly one commit, so any running container can be traced to its code.
TAG="$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"

# 5. WHAT: warn if this is not an Apple Silicon Mac.
#    WHY: we build for ARM64 (AWS Graviton, cheaper). On an Intel/AMD machine Docker emulates
#    ARM, which works but is much slower.
HOST_ARCH="$(uname -m)"
if [ "$HOST_ARCH" != "arm64" ] && [ "$HOST_ARCH" != "aarch64" ]; then
  echo "WARNING: this machine is $HOST_ARCH, not ARM. The ARM64 build will use emulation and be slower." >&2
fi

# 6. WHAT: use the same region as Pulumi, unless the caller already set it. The AWS credentials

# @concept: arm64-graviton
# @concept: same-origin-routing
# 9. WHAT: build for linux/arm64 and push in one step (--push): api, web, then the worker (S1c).
#    WHY: the ECS tasks (Step 11e) will run on ARM64, and an image only runs on the CPU it
#    was built for. buildx is Docker's multi-platform builder.
#    --provenance=false: stops buildx adding extra "attestation" manifests, so each tag is
#    one plain image and `describe-images` shows a single clean ARM64 image.
#    web gets no NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: empty means same origin (see docs/16-infra-ecr.md).
echo "Building and pushing api:$TAG ..."
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \
  -f apps/api/Dockerfile -t "$API_REPO:$TAG" --push .

echo "Building and pushing web:$TAG ..."
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \
  -f apps/web/Dockerfile -t "$WEB_REPO:$TAG" --push .

# @concept: arm64-graviton
# @concept: same-origin-routing
# 9. WHAT: build for linux/arm64 and push in one step (--push): api, web, then the worker (S1c).
#    WHY: the ECS tasks (Step 11e) will run on ARM64, and an image only runs on the CPU it
#    was built for. buildx is Docker's multi-platform builder.
#    --provenance=false: stops buildx adding extra "attestation" manifests, so each tag is
#    one plain image and `describe-images` shows a single clean ARM64 image.
#    web gets no NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: empty means same origin (see docs/16-infra-ecr.md).
echo "Building and pushing api:$TAG ..."
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \
  -f apps/api/Dockerfile -t "$API_REPO:$TAG" --push .

echo "Building and pushing web:$TAG ..."
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \
  -f apps/web/Dockerfile -t "$WEB_REPO:$TAG" --push .

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# @concept: migrations
# Runs the database migrations on AWS as a one-off ECS task, waits for it, and reports.
# Run from anywhere:  pnpm infra:migrate   (locally: export AWS_PROFILE=ticketlite first)
# CD runs the SAME script between its two phases (.github/workflows/cd.yml, Step 12b).
# Needs the data AND compute layers on (the cluster and task definition are part of compute).
# Explained in docs/17-infra-ecs-api.md.

# 1. WHAT: stop at the first error, on unset variables, and in failed pipes.
#    WHY: a half-finished run must never look like a success.
set -euo pipefail

# 2. WHAT: work from the repo root, wherever the script was started.
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"

# 3. WHAT: use the same region as Pulumi, unless the caller already set it. The AWS credentials come
#    from the environment: locally `export AWS_PROFILE=ticketlite`, in CD the OIDC role.

# @concept: fargate-spot
# 6. WHAT: start ONE task from the migration task definition (infra/src/compute/migration-task.ts):
#    the api image, command `node dist/migrate.js`, the DB settings, in the api's subnets and
#    security group (the database lets in only that group).
#    WHICH image: normally the deployed tag (the same code as the api). During a CD deploy, phase A
#    points it at the NEW image first, so the new code's SQL files run BEFORE the services roll.
#    (Until Step 12b this borrowed the api task definition with a command override; its own task
#    definition is what lets its image differ from the api's.)
#    --launch-type FARGATE (not Spot): a migration must not be interrupted halfway. It runs
#    for seconds, so the price difference is nothing.
#    --started-by: a label, so this task is easy to spot in the console.
echo "Starting the migration task in cluster $CLUSTER ..."
TASK_ARN="$(aws ecs run-task \
  --cluster "$CLUSTER" \
  --task-definition "$TASK_DEF" \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
